1:
Who is bidden arise they do not agree on. Gill notes the versions that supply the city's name, and takes the address for the Jewish church as distinct from the Gentiles, since these are afterwards said to come to it: the Jews converted at last, called out of a long dejection. Wesley reads it as a type instead, the Hebrew idiom making prostration a servile and calamitous condition and rising a recovery out of it, so that under the figure of one city's restoration what stands displayed is the flourishing state of the Gentile church. Clarke joins the two, taking the period when Jew and Gentile become one fold under one Shepherd, and thinks the prospect lifted the prophet above even his usual majesty. Ellicott keeps to the vision: a new Jerusalem seen under the forms of the old, prostrate as though in the underworld, and now summoned to fresh life.

What that radiance amounts to Henry works out in two registers. Historically, the return from captivity brought gladness and honour, and the Redeemer coming to Zion brought day with him and became himself its source. Theologically, God stands as the father and fountain of lights, and only in his beams do we see at all, so that our morning has come so far as we have knowledge of him within and favour from him without: when he appears to us we enjoy the comfort of that favour and the glory rises like dawn, and when he appears for us we have the credit of it and the glory rests visibly upon us, as in the pillar of cloud and fire. Wesley reduces the whole to a flourishing and prosperous condition, Gill to the shining of Christ and the Gospel, held forth in profession and conversation.

What the darkness means divides Keil and Delitzsch from everyone else. Gill takes it for ignorance, idolatry, superstition and false worship, and surveys his own century: heathen gloom here, Mahometan there, papal elsewhere, the Gospel on a very small spot and dim even there, a dusk in which morning has yet to break. Clarke says shortly that such was the condition of the Gentile peoples, Wesley that all kinds of error are meant, Ellicott that the veil which once shrouded Zion still hangs over the heathen who are to share her brightness. Keil and Delitzsch reject the whole reading. The gloom settling upon the world of nations must not be understood as ignorance or enmity against God at all; the passage runs on from the judgment described before, so that after those judgments have passed, blackness at its deepest still covers the ground and a canopy of cloud the peoples. It remains night as on the first day, but a night appointed to give place to morning.

The same voice supplies the governing image. If darkness lies everywhere and must break, the question becomes where the sun will rise; and the answer runs that Zion herself is the east, in which this sun of suns comes up. Gill offers a second construction beside his first, that the obscurity may be the confusion of the antichristian states at the moment their overthrow begins.

On the coming of the nations they divide by tense. Wesley calls it a plain prophecy of their calling. Gill has them drawn to the Gospel preached in her midst, and to Christ who enlightens her, and into her church state. Clarke alone says it has in some sort already happened: those peoples received the Gospel from that land, their kings embraced it, and many realms are full of the doctrine, though he holds the full completion of terms so ample and exalted reserved for later times.
4:
The carried daughters put two of them on the same custom by different roads. Clarke reaches it through the apparatus: where the received text has nursed at the side, the Greek and the Aramaic read carried, one manuscript has carried on the shoulder, another has both words; and he settles the sense by a traveller's note that in the east children ride astride the hip with the arm round the body. Ellicott gives the same custom directly, the child on the mother's hip with arms clasped round her waist. Keil and Delitzsch have them clinging to the side of those who carry them.

Whether Zion is to see or to fear is a textual dispute on two different principles. Clarke counts witnesses and then argues from the poetry: forty manuscripts of one collator and twenty-eight of another read thou shalt fear, and the parallelism confirms it, the heart ruffled and dilated in the second line answering to the fear and joy in the first. Ellicott reports the same variant as adopted by many. Keil and Delitzsch weigh the external evidence the other way: the reading from the verb to see is favoured by the ancient versions, by all the earlier Jewish commentators but one, and by the Masoretic text itself.

The emotion they describe alike. Gill has a flow of joy like a river's stream, or a heart beating and fluttering with surprise. Keil and Delitzsch make it the greatest delight mingled with trembling, the heart trembling and expanding at once. Ellicott renders the verb literally as throb, an awe-stricken joy at the marvellous prosperity, followed by the expansion of ecstasy. Wesley says enlarged both with joy and love.

The tribes named are identified in three registers. Gill traces Midian to a son of Abraham by Keturah and the other two names to sons of Ishmael, whose twelve sons held the country from the Euphrates to the Red Sea, and then applies it to his own day: these design the Turks and Saracens, to be converted now. Ellicott keeps to history: Nebaioth expanded before the Christian era into the kingdom of the Nabathaean Arabs, from the gulf to the Hauran, the two names together covering what the Roman geographers called the two Arabias. Wesley types it, since the queen who visited Solomon came from one of these countries and brought gifts, and Solomon was a type of Christ.

The rams that minister draw the prettiest note. Clarke reports a commentator who takes their going up on the altar as a voluntary offering, the victims waiting for no priest but presenting themselves freely, which he thinks gives a very elegant turn to the image; and he supports it from the heathen notion that a victim brought without reluctance was a good omen and one that broke away a bad one. Wesley keeps to the word acceptance: they shall not now, as heretofore, be rejected, and takes the sacrifices offered and accepted as a type of how glorious the New Testament worship shall be.

The cloud and the doves divide the allegorist from the observer. Gill takes the cloud four ways: for the number of the converts, covering the land as clouds cover the heavens; for their elevation from an earthly state to a heavenly; for their being filled with grace as clouds with water; and for their unanimity, coming together in one body openly. Ellicott sees ships, the cloud-like sails bringing the exiles home, hastening like doves to the dove-cote. Keil and Delitzsch mark the structure instead, this being where the third movement begins: after glorification by the rising of the glory and by the recovery of the scattered children comes that by the nations' service. Henry puts the whole sequence on one ground: all the favour the people of God find with men is owing to the light of his countenance towards them.
10:
Who the builders are is read two ways. Gill takes them for Gentiles once strangers to the covenants and aliens from the commonwealth, converted in great numbers and made useful in building up the church and defending it; Wesley says they shall administer all necessaries. Ellicott allows the willing proselyte but sets a second possibility beside it, that they are brought into subjection, since to build the temples and palaces of conquerors was, as in the Egyptian and Babylonian bondage, the almost inevitable lot of the conquered. He keeps the darker sense at the gates too, where the verb used of the kings implies that they are brought as captives, acknowledging the sovereignty of Zion with or against their will.

The open gates carry three senses for Gill: a peaceable state, with no enemy to fear and so no concern to shut them; a vast concourse always coming in; and a capacity that is never filled, since however many come there will still be room. Ellicott gets the first two and adds the detail of caravans of pilgrims with their offerings entering by night as well as day, and notes with interest that the thought is transferred in the last book to the heavenly city. Gill alone supplies the counterpart, the nation that will not serve, which he identifies with those who set another head over themselves and reject the authority of Christ.

What comes from Lebanon divides the literal from the figurative. Ellicott sees a revival of the glories of Solomon's days, the cedars and other trees furnishing timber for the buildings or else planted in the courts and open places, and takes the box for a species of cedar. Keil and Delitzsch make the trees living too, dug up with their roots rather than felled, and mark the turn from what is great in the world of men to what is great in the world of nature. Gill and Wesley allegorise them into persons: as the cedars went into the old temple, so men eminent for gifts and graces, drawn with the cords of love, come into the church, durable and ever green, pillars that shall never go out.

The place of God's feet they identify differently. Clarke makes it the ark, since the visible appearance the Jews called the shechinah rested between the cherubim above it, and a footstool is a necessary appendage to a throne; Wesley says the same. Ellicott takes it as clearly parallel with the sanctuary of the previous clause, and notes that the word footstool is used elsewhere of the temple itself. On the sons of the afflicters, Keil and Delitzsch hold that the persecutors are now no more and their children feel themselves disarmed, seized with shame when they see the church they tormented so exalted. Ellicott names that as the common explanation and prefers another, the law of inherited retribution which entered so largely into the Hebrew's thought of the moral government of the world. Wesley allows that the Hebrew idiom may mean the men themselves, and Gill runs through three candidates: the posterity of the first persecutors, the descendants of the Roman heathen, or those called out of papal Rome at her destruction.
15:
How thoroughly she had been abandoned they set out together, and one gets structure out of it. Henry has a city her friends abandoned and her enemies abhorred, which no man went through but declined as a rueful spectacle. Ellicott sees a forsaken and slighted wife mingling with the literal picture of a city in ruins. Keil and Delitzsch separate the two ideas the name Zion carries, a church and a metropolis: forsaken and hated fit either, but no one walked through thee fits only the desolate city, so the church prevails in one verse and the city in the next. Henry adds the caution that governs the rest: the city's excellency was short and came far short of the vast compass of this promise.

The milk of the nations is a bold figure, softened two ways. Ellicott grants the boldness, notes the prophet had put it less startlingly before, and takes the sense to be that the new city will be supported by Gentile offerings. Wesley keeps the image and turns it kind: the wealth of nations and the power of kings will come freely, as milk flows from a mother's breast.

The exchange of materials divides the allegorist from the historian. Gill reads the four terms as three dispensations: wood and stones the old covenant, brass and iron the present gospel, silver and gold the glory to come, silver for the spiritual reign and gold for the personal one in a city of pure gold down to its street; and as far as brass exceeds wood, so far does the gospel exceed the law. Ellicott sets it against the wealth of Solomon's reign and finds one striking difference: there the king's officers and exactors were instruments of oppression, here the very embodiment of righteousness and peace. Wesley makes the same allusion in four words: such even thy tax-gatherers shall be.

The named walls draw the best piece of antiquarianism. Ellicott recalls the eastern practice of giving city walls names implying a consecration, and cites the two divine names borne by the walls of Babylon. On the violence he differs by direction: following the verse before, he sees freedom from internal misgovernment rather than external invasion, where Gill hears the end of antichristian persecution. Wesley dates the whole to the thousand years of Christ's reign on earth.

The failing lights produce a textual repair and a distinction. Clarke thinks the line defective, since the Greek and the Aramaic both express by night, which is needed to answer to by day in the line before; he would either substitute that word for by brightness or add it. Ellicott lets sun and moon go on shining and says only that they will not be needed in a greater radiance, since on earth the sun sets and the moon wanes, and there no waning and no setting. Gill makes a distinction nobody else makes: the sun of the next verse is not the sun of this one but the church's own, the sun of righteousness, who has risings and settings now, at least in his people's apprehension, but will not have them then.

Two closing questions. Gill will not let all righteous pass loosely: the Lord's people always were and will be so, but the members of churches have not been, since Israel had only a remnant, the disciples had a Judas, one church a pair who lied and another many disorderly, and foolish virgins have been among the wise in every age. Ellicott takes the little one not numerically but for a clan or subdivision of a tribe; Keil and Delitzsch allow growth by extension of fellowship as well as by children. Clarke ends on the hastening and draws the distinction carefully: the time set must come before anything begins, so it is not the appointed time that is hastened but every circumstance of the event once begun.
